soil-fert-001.title: Fertilizer, the material behind up to half of every harvest
soil-fert-001.text: Conservative estimates credit fertilizers with 30 to 50% of what crops yield. A fertilizer is any natural or synthetic material applied to soil or to plant tissues to supply plant nutrients, the elements described in {{ref:soil-fert-181}}. That supply is what sets it apart from acid-correcting materials and other additions that bring no nutrients. Modern fertilization centers on three macronutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Ground rock, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-075}}, sometimes supplements them with micronutrients. Most fertilizers work by feeding the plant, but some also improve the soil's water-holding capacity and aeration. Before synthetic products, farmers kept their land fertile with decomposed organic waste, animal and human dung, mined minerals, rotating crops and by-products such as fish waste or bloodmeal. How much to apply depends on the crop and on {{ref:soil-fert-149}}, usually measured by a soil test. Legumes fix their own nitrogen and generally need no nitrogen fertilizer. The scale is vast. In 2023 agriculture used 190 million tonnes of inorganic fertilizer nutrients, and 112 million tonnes of that, 58%, was nitrogen. Excess carries a price. Nutrients washed off fields pollute water and overfeed it, the process in {{ref:soil-env-020}}, and some mined fertilizers add heavy metals to soil.

soil-fert-028.title: Compost, waste turned back into living soil
soil-fert-028.text: About a fifth of landfill waste is food and other material that could have rotted usefully elsewhere. Decaying without oxygen in a landfill, it releases methane. Compost is the alternative: a mixture of decomposed organic materials used as plant fertilizer and to improve the soil's physical, chemical and biological properties. It forms when plant and food waste, recycled organic materials and animal dung break down, the process of {{ref:soil-bio-115}}. The finished product teems with life, from bacteria and fungi to protozoa and nematodes. Worked into the ground, it feeds crops, conditions the soil and adds organic matter, raising its humus or humic acid content. Its microbes widen the soil's microbial diversity and suppress pathogens and soil-borne diseases. Gardens, horticulture, urban agriculture and {{ref:soil-agri-135}} use it to depend less on chemical fertilizers. Compost also reclaims land and streams, helps construct new marshland and covers landfills. Decomposing waste in heaps and long rows is also one way to clean polluted ground, the approach in {{ref:soil-env-023}}. Alkaline soils containing solid calcium carbonate can be reclaimed by working in compost and other acidifying organic materials. The practice is old. Cato the Elder described it in 160 BCE, in the early Roman Empire, and the first industrial compost station opened in Wels, Austria, in 1921.

soil-fert-063.title: Soil conditioners loosen, feed and rebalance the ground
soil-fert-063.text: Compacted soil can starve a plant that sits among plenty, because its roots struggle to take up water and nutrients. Loosening it is the most common job of a soil conditioner. That is a material added to soil to improve its physical qualities, usually its fertility and sometimes its mechanics. Conditioners are usually seen as a subset of soil amendments, a broader category that also takes in many fertilizers and non-organic materials. Examples range from straw, peat, vermiculite and sulfur to water-absorbing polymers, compost and {{ref:soil-fert-050}}. Many add carbon, nitrogen, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus, and amendments can greatly raise cation-exchange capacity. Organic material can greatly improve water retention in sandy soils. Conditioners can also adjust pH for particular plants, or make very acid or alkaline soils usable. A soil test should come first, to show which one suits the soil. Too much harms plants through excess salts, nitrogen and metals, and surplus nutrients can run off into waterways. Builders use the same idea under another name, described in {{ref:soil-agri-076}}.

soil-fert-066.title: Mulch, a blanket laid over the soil
soil-fert-066.text: A layer just 5 centimetres (2 in) deep can change what happens beneath it. Mulch is a layer of material applied to the surface of soil, and such layers are normally that deep or deeper. It conserves {{ref:soil-water-155}}, improves fertility and soil health, suppresses weeds, regulates soil temperature and makes beds look better. Mulch is usually organic but not always. Plastic sheeting is permanent; bark chips are temporary. Early in the season, mulch keeps in heat that would otherwise escape at night, warming the soil enough for earlier sowing. Later it steadies both temperature and moisture. It cuts evaporation, but it can also catch light rain, and overly thick layers can reduce oxygen in the soil. On slopes it is laid to prevent erosion. Worms and other organisms work mulches of compost and animal dung into the soil on their own. The choice of material weighs availability, cost, appearance, effects on soil chemistry and pH, durability, decomposition rate and freedom from weed seeds and pathogens.

soil-fert-050.title: Biochar, charcoal made to be buried
soil-fert-050.text: Charcoal made for the soil can persist there for thousands of years. Biochar is a form of {{ref:soil-class-083}}, sometimes modified, made by heating biomass with little oxygen. What remains after this pyrolysis is a light, black residue of carbon and ash. It is sterile when made and comes alive only after soil organisms reach it. Farmers add it mainly to improve aeration and fertility, cut greenhouse gas emissions and nutrient leaching, and reduce acidity. It may also raise the water content of coarse soils. Too much, or a feedstock unsuited to the soil, can harm soil organisms, reduce available water, alter pH and raise salinity. The word, joining the Greek bios, life, with char, dates from the late 20th century, but the practice is older. Pre-Columbian Amazonians smoldered farm waste under soil in pits or trenches, and settlers called the result terra preta. Whether those farmers meant to improve the soil is unknown. Beyond soils, biochar goes into animal feed, concrete mixes and water treatment, where it removes heavy metals, dyes and organic pollutants.

soil-fert-014.title: The hidden bill for feeding the world's crops
soil-fert-014.text: Fertilizer washing off farmland helps create dead zones in the ocean. That is one of the direct costs of fertilizers, whose production and use harm water, soil, air and ecosystems. It also contaminates waterways, the soil microbiome degrades and toxic compounds accumulate. Indirect costs reach further: nitrogen-crop-pest cascades, fracking for the gas the Haber process needs, and the biodiversity and soil loss tied to industrial agriculture. The climate pays too. Most synthetic fertilizer depends on fossil fuel, with methane supplying the hydrogen for ammonia. The IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Land names fertilizer production and its associated land use among the drivers of global warming. Organic sources are not blameless, since too much pig slurry can contaminate aquifers and overfeed the waters they supply. Solar energy, waste treatment and electrolysis are proposed alternatives for production. On the farm, plowing less and planting buffer strips can lessen the damage. Policy favors sustainable or regenerative farming, with less synthetic fertilizer, better care of the soil and more of the biological fertilizers in {{ref:soil-fert-010}}.

soil-fert-011.title: Feeding the crop when it is hungry
soil-fert-011.text: A crop's appetite is not constant. Its nutrient uptake peaks from early to mid-season, so fertilizer applied near seeding works well. Fertilizer timing means matching when and how much fertilizer goes on to the crop's needs, the weather and the type of farming, a core part of {{ref:soil-fert-192}}. Hitting peak demand is essential for both yield and quality. For fall-planted grains such as winter wheat, autumn nitrogen followed by a spring topdressing is likely the best combination. Weather matters too. Soluble fertilizers such as {{ref:soil-fert-071}} are not applied during heavy rain, which would carry most of it away and pollute the aquifer. Farms practicing {{ref:soil-agri-065}}, and smallholdings, cut mineral fertilizer to the crop's strict needs, sometimes to none. After harvest, a fast-growing, nitrogen-hungry crop such as white mustard can take up leftover nitrate before it reaches groundwater. Buried afterward, it forms humus.

soil-fert-002.title: From ancient dung to factory nitrogen
soil-fert-002.text: Egyptians, Romans, Babylonians and early Germans all left records of using minerals or animal dung to make their farms more productive. The industry came much later. {{ref:soil-hist-004}} is often called the father of the fertilizer industry, although scientific study of plant nutrition began before him. In 1837 {{ref:soil-hist-074}} began testing fertilizing materials on potted plants. In 1842 he patented phosphates treated with sulfuric acid, founding the artificial fertilizer industry. He and Joseph Henry Gilbert then ran crop experiments together at the Institute of Arable Crops Research. Industrial nitrogen began with processes such as Birkeland–Eyde, which fixed atmospheric nitrogen into nitric acid. The Haber and Ostwald processes rose in the 1910s and 1920s. After World War II, nitrogen plants expanded for bomb making were turned to farm use. Between 1961 and 2019 nitrogen fertilizer use grew 800%, a crucial part of the farm productivity gains described in {{ref:soil-agri-138}}. Phosphate use climbed from 9 million tonnes a year in 1960 to 40 million in 2000.

soil-fert-003.title: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium: the big three of fertilizer
soil-fert-003.text: Three letters, NPK, sum up most of what fertilizers deliver: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Fertilizers supply these in varying proportions, along with micronutrients. Each has its own job. Nitrogen drives leaf and stem growth. Phosphorus builds roots, flowers, seeds and fruit. Potassium gives strong stems and aids water movement, flowering and fruiting. None is applied as a pure element; fertilizers are compounds that contain them. Nitrogen matters most, as part of proteins, DNA and chlorophyll. The air holds plenty of it, but in a form plants cannot use. Plants get it from weathering of nitrogen-bearing rocks and from bacteria that fix it, some free-living and some in legume roots. Phosphate goes into DNA, the energy carrier ATP and the phospholipids of cell membranes. Macronutrients make up 0.15% to 6.0% of plant dry matter. Overfertilized plants take up more than they need, a habit called luxury consumption. Calcium, long thought a luxury, is now considered essential for keeping cell walls and membranes intact.

soil-fert-004.title: Sorting fertilizers by nutrient count and origin
soil-fert-004.text: Every fertilizer sits on two scales at once: how many nutrients it carries, and where it came from. On the first scale, straight fertilizers supply a single nutrient such as N, P or K. Multinutrient, or complex, fertilizers supply two or more. NP fertilizers supply nitrogen and phosphorus together. Monoammonium phosphate, or MAP, holds 11% N and 48% P2O5; diammonium phosphate, or DAP, holds 18% N and 46% P2O5. NPK fertilizers supply all three main nutrients, in two styles. Compound NPKs bind the nutrients chemically, while blends are physical mixtures of single-nutrient fertilizers. The second scale is origin. Inorganic fertilizers exclude carbon-bearing materials, except {{ref:soil-fert-021}}. They are also called synthetic, because chemical treatments are needed to make them. The other class, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-010}}, is usually recycled plant- or animal-derived matter such as compost or animal dung. Solubility also differs between products. More than 90% of a typical {{ref:soil-fert-094}} dissolves in water, against about 85% of MAP and DAP.

soil-fert-007.title: Nitrogen fertilizer, pulled from the air by industry
soil-fert-007.text: About a third of the world's annual food production relies on ammonia from the {{ref:soil-fert-104}}, supporting nearly half the world's population. Nitrogen fertilizers are made from that ammonia. In this energy-intensive process, natural gas usually supplies the hydrogen and the air supplies the nitrogen. The ammonia is then the feedstock for other fertilizers, such as {{ref:soil-fert-071}} and {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, and the Ostwald process turns it into nitrates. That salt of ammonium and nitrate carries 34-35% nitrogen. Blended with limestone or dolomite, it carries 24-28%. Sodium nitrate, or Chilean saltpeter, from the Atacama Desert was one of the first nitrogen fertilizers, used from 1830 and still mined. In 2012 the world used about 110 million tons of nitrogen fertilizer a year. Only part becomes plant matter; the rest accumulates in the soil or washes away. In soil, bacteria such as Nitrosomonas oxidize ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate, which dissolves readily and is easily leached.

soil-fert-021.title: Urea, from urine and the laboratory to the field
soil-fert-021.text: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from inorganic starting materials, contradicting the doctrine of vitalism. Urea is a simple organic nitrogen compound, CO(NH2)2, found in mammal urine. More than 90% of the world's industrial urea now goes onto fields as a nitrogen-release fertilizer. At 45-46% nitrogen, it has the highest nitrogen content of the common solid nitrogen fertilizers. That makes it cheap to transport per unit of nitrogen, and it is non-explosive. In the soil, bacteria with the enzyme urease convert it to ammonium, which roots take up. In some soils, bacteria then oxidize the ammonium to nitrate. Nitrogen lost to the air or washed away is wasteful and harmful, so urea is coated in inert sealants or converted to urea-formaldehyde compounds that release nitrogen slowly. Urea washed off fertilized land may help make algal blooms toxic. Biuret, the most common impurity in synthetic urea, impairs plant growth. Where it is cheap, urea also reduces soil alkalinity: ammonium from its hydrolysis displaces sodium from the soil's exchange sites.

soil-fert-010.title: Organic fertilizers: plant food from living things
soil-fert-010.text: Seaweed, feathers and treated sewage can all feed a crop. Organic fertilizers are fertilizers of biological origin, derived from living or formerly living materials, the stuff of {{ref:soil-bio-114}}. They include animal wastes, crop wastes, seaweed, compost and treated sewage sludge, the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-045}}. Slaughter adds bloodmeal, feather meal and {{ref:soil-fert-090}}. The term also covers packaged products that meet the rules of {{ref:soil-agri-135}}, which limit or avoid synthetic fertilizers and pesticides. Sewage sludge may be unacceptable there, because of residual contaminants and public perception. Most organic fertilizers hold less-concentrated nutrients that are harder to quantify, but they can build soil. Compost can raise nutrient availability by improving cation-exchange capacity or by boosting microbes that free nutrients. Peat, the most used packaged organic amendment, improves aeration and moisture but adds no nutrients, so it is an amendment rather than a fertilizer. Fresh sawdust can draw down soil nitrogen as wood-decay fungi colonize it, which can also capture excess mineral nitrogen.

soil-fert-023.title: Manure, the oldest way to feed a field
soil-fert-023.text: Long before factories made fertilizer, Egyptians, Romans, Babylonians and early Germans were recorded using manure or minerals to make their farms more productive. Manure is organic matter, mostly animal feces, used as organic fertilizer in agriculture. In managing soil today it stands beside two other main classes: compost and {{ref:soil-fert-026}}. Manure builds fertility through a chain. It adds organic matter and nutrients such as nitrogen. Those feed soil bacteria and fungi, which in turn feed the rest of the soil food web. Like compost or mulch, it can also change a soil's {{ref:soil-fert-184}}. Long manuring leaves a lasting mark in the soil profile. Anthrosols of northwestern Europe often carry plaggic or terric horizons, built this way, across some 500,000 hectares. Language has shifted too. The term artificial manure, once in wide use, meant what are now called artificial fertilizers. Manure has also become a product: it is composted, bagged and sold as a soil amendment.

soil-fert-026.title: Green manure, a crop grown to be plowed under
soil-fert-026.text: Greek farmers were plowing beans into the soil by about 300 BC, and the Romans used faba beans and lupines. Colonists later carried the practice to North America. Green manure is a crop grown specifically to be worked into the soil while still green. Its biomass is plowed or disced in, as with ordinary manure, mainly to add organic matter. Legumes such as clover and vetch are favorites, because their root-nodule bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, as described in {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Depending on the species, 45 to 224 kg/ha (40 to 200 lb/acre) of nitrogen is released. Usually 40-60% of the green crop's nitrogen becomes available to the next crop. Decay also releases phosphorus, potassium and sulfur, and deep-rooted species bring up nutrients that shallower crops cannot reach. The added organic matter, microbial mycelium and sticky substances improve aggregation, infiltration, water retention and aeration. While growing, the crop suppresses weeds, helps control erosion and feeds pollinators. In alkali soils it lowers pH by generating humic acid.

soil-fert-076.title: Carbon farming: putting the air's carbon back in the field
soil-fert-076.text: Turning forest, grassland or savanna into cropland cuts the organic carbon in its soil by about 30–40%, largely because harvests remove carbon-bearing plant material. Carbon farming tries to reverse that. It is a set of methods that aim to store carbon in soil and biomass, for a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere. Farmers change how they plow, graze and choose crops, spread compost or plant-based mulch, and work with biochar and terra preta. Leaving harvest residues, applying manure or rotating in deep-rooted perennial crops all add carbon back. The gains are reversible. Disturbance or heavy plowing turns soil into a greenhouse gas source, and after several decades soils saturate and stop absorbing carbon. The method costs US$3–130 per tonne of CO2 sequestered, depending on region. Some claims remain disputed: many researchers question the carbon benefits claimed for {{ref:soil-env-090}}, and the effect of added carbon on yields is not settled.

soil-fert-059.title: Agricultural lime, crushed rock against acid soil
soil-fert-059.text: Soils turn acid in three main ways: leaching under high rainfall, crops removing minerals, and the reactions of modern chemical fertilizers. Agricultural lime is a common answer. It is pulverized limestone or chalk whose main active component is calcium carbonate. Unlike quicklime and slaked lime, ground limestone needs no burning in a kiln, only milling. All these limes supply a base that corrects acidity. Lime raises the pH of acid soils, supplies calcium, helps water penetrate, and improves plant uptake of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Still, lime is not a fertilizer, though it can be used together with one. Dolomitic lime acts similarly but supplies magnesium as well as calcium. A soil test is the best way to tell whether a soil is acid or short of calcium or magnesium. Fields once usually received burnt lime instead, because affordable fine milling of stone only developed after the mid-19th century. Wood ash, magnesium oxide, basic slag, silicate rock dust and oyster shells also raise soil pH.

soil-fert-055.title: Liming: calcium against the aluminum in acid soil
soil-fert-055.text: Most acid soils are saturated not with hydrogen ions but with aluminum, and their acidity generally comes from aluminum hydrolysis. Liming answers that by adding calcium- and magnesium-rich materials such as chalk, limestone, burnt lime, hydrated lime or {{ref:soil-fert-079}}. In acid soils these act as a base and neutralize acidity, often improving plant growth and soil bacterial activity. Oversupply, though, can harm plants. Sandy, heavily leached or strongly acid mineral soils are low in calcium and need liming most. It can also offset the poor cation-exchange capacity that lets potassium leach away. Raising the pH frequently relieves molybdenum deficiency by decreasing molybdenum sorption. Not every effect is welcome. A German forestry study comparing stands two and twenty years after liming found it washed more nitrate out of the soil and lowered phosphorus in some leaves. Before modern liming, farmers spread raw chalk and lime debris, a practice with evidence dating to the 1200s in the British Isles.

soil-fert-073.title: Leachate, the liquid that carries a material away
soil-fert-073.text: Rain falling on a landfill does not leave it clean. Leachate is any liquid that passes through a material and carries away its dissolved or suspended components. In environmental science, the word means a liquid carrying harmful substances that can enter the environment, most often from landfills. Compost sites produce it in wet periods, as rain washes decomposed matter away. Stockpiled coal and mine wastes yield it when exposed sulfide minerals form sulfuric acid, often rich in metals. Acidic leachate flushed from acid sulfate soils can harm groundwater and surface waters, with effects that may persist or peak after dry spells.

soil-fert-072.title: Perlite, volcanic glass that swells in the heat
soil-fert-072.text: Heated to 850–900 °C, perlite swells to 7–16 times its original volume. Perlite is an amorphous volcanic glass, usually formed by hydration of obsidian. The heat vaporizes its trapped water and leaves a brilliant white material. As a soil amendment it is highly permeable, holds little water and helps prevent compaction. On its own it serves for hydroponics and for rooting cuttings. In potting mixes, perlite and vermiculite improve aeration and water retention. Cacti and succulents need a large share of perlite or sand for drainage.

soil-fert-034.title: How much compost a field really needs
soil-fert-034.text: A field needs only a thin coat: about 6 mm (0.24 in) of compost, broadcast and worked in before planting. Rebuilding poor soil or controlling erosion takes 25 mm (0.98 in) or more. Compost application is the use of finished compost on fields, in beds and in growing mixes to add organic matter and nutrients. Ready compost is dark brown or black, with an earthy smell. Added to soil, peat or {{ref:soil-agri-139}}, it improves tilth and supplies humus and nutrients. Tilled in, it raises organic matter and overall fertility, and it can increase plant immunity to diseases and pests. It is rarely used alone. Growers mix it with sand, grit, bark, vermiculite, perlite or clay granules, and blends of 20–30% compost are common for transplanting seedlings. Sowing seed straight into compost is unwise. It dries fast, immature compost may hold phytotoxins that inhibit germination, and undecomposed lignin may tie up nitrogen.

soil-fert-029.title: Inside a compost heap: carbon, nitrogen, air and water
soil-fert-029.text: A well-run compost heap holds itself at 54–71 °C (130–160 °F) until its materials are broken down. Composting is the aerobic decomposition of organic solid wastes into compost, a humus-like material. Its organisms need four ingredients. Carbon gives energy, and its oxidation releases heat. Nitrogen lets them grow. Oxygen oxidizes the carbon. Water must be plentiful, but never waterlogging. Aerobic bacteria need oxygen above 5%, so heaps are turned to keep up both oxygen and the right moisture. Bacteria and fungi convert the inputs into heat, carbon dioxide and ammonium ions, and over months the materials become humus. The recipe hinges on the {{ref:soil-fert-184}}. Composting runs most efficiently at about 25:1. Above 30 the mix is starved of nitrogen; below 15 it tends to lose nitrogen as ammonia. Green waste such as grass, leaves and food scraps supplies nitrogen. Brown waste such as stalks, paper and wood chips supplies carbon. Fresh grass sits near 15:1, dry autumn leaves near 50:1. On farms, manure is the usual nitrogen source and bedding such as straw or sawdust the carbon source. Poultry manure needs blending with high-carbon materials, and wet pig manure with straw.

openers.fertilizers-manures-and-amendments: Farmers have fed their fields for thousands of years, first with animal dung and minerals and, from the 19th century, with the products of a synthetic fertilizer industry. This chapter is about what people add to soil, and why. Most additions supply nutrients, chiefly nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and much of the nitrogen comes from ammonia made by the Haber–Bosch process. Other additions work on the soil itself: decomposed organic waste, a protective layer over the surface, charcoal made for burial, and materials that loosen and improve the ground. The chapter also weighs the harm fertilizers do to water, soil, air and ecosystems, and how matching their timing and amount to a crop's needs can limit it.
